header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp734.tmp734.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Several scriptural citations in the edition are faulty and are given here as corrected references where evident: 'Psal. CXXVIII, 8' is Ps. 138 (Vulgate); 'II Reg. XII, 9' is II Kings (II Sam.) xxii, 9; 'Thren. I, 18' (Lamentations) is attributed in the text to Isaiah. 'MMM ejus' is read as 'oculis ejus' (to his eyes), and 'osa.' as 'Coloss.'. The Latin 'posteriora' is rendered 'back parts'.

Deut. reference printed as xxxiii, 5; the verse is xxxiii, 3. Gen. i, 51 corrected to i, 31. In the second passage 'quam ipse illos indurat' is evidently 'quasi ipse...' or similar; rendered 'he is said himself to harden them'. 'Cherubim' interpreted as 'fullness of knowledge'; the Latin 'plenitudo sive multitudo' is rendered as alternatives. The Proverbs quotation ('The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom') is not in canonical Proverbs; it is a common patristic attribution.

Read 'in homine' for the printed 'in nomine' (likeness of God 'in man'), 'sum' for the garbled 'MMM', and 'est' for 'cal'. In the list of names for the soul, 'natura' is odd and may be corrupt (perhaps for 'mens', mind); translated as printed.

nodes.text: ON THE ESSENCE OF THE DIVINITY: ONE BOOK.

I. Almighty God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, is one and three: one, that is, in nature, but three in persons. He alone is invisible, he alone is immeasurable and incomprehensible, he alone is uncircumscribed, he alone is unchangeable, incorporeal and immortal, present everywhere but hidden, everywhere whole but immeasurable. He is invisible, because in his essence he cannot be seen, as the Apostle testifies, who says, Whom no man has seen, nor can see (I Tim. vi, 16). And in the Gospel, No one has ever seen God (John i, 18). He is incorporeal, because he does not exist composed or put together from any outlines of limbs, as the Truth says in the Gospel, God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (ibid. iv, 24). He is immeasurable, because his quantity or quality cannot be measured by any of the creatures; Solomon, entreating him in his prayer, says to him, If heaven and the heavens of heavens do not contain you, how much less this house which I have built (III Kings viii, 27)? He is uncircumscribed, since he cannot be circumscribed. He is not in place, since he in no way passes from place to place, nor is he held in any place whatever; he himself bears witness of himself through the prophet Isaiah and says, Heaven is my seat, and the earth the footstool of my feet (Isa. lxvi, 1). And through Jeremiah, Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord (Jer. xxiii, 24)? Confessing his immeasurability, the prophet says to God himself in the Psalm, If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present (Ps. cxxxviii, 8). Of his immeasurability it is further written in the book of blessed Job, He is higher than heaven, and what will you do? Deeper than hell, and how will you know (Job xi, 8)? His measure is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea. For he who fills heaven and earth, beyond doubt, there is no place absent from his presence. For he presides over all creation by ruling and commanding; he is beneath all things by sustaining and carrying [them], not with the weight of toil, but with untiring power; since no creature made by him can subsist by itself unless it is sustained by him who created it. He is outside all things, but not shut out; he is within all things, but not shut in. He is unchangeable, because he cannot at all be changed from what he is, as he himself says through the prophet Malachi, I am the Lord and I do not change (Mal. iii, 6). And God is called unchangeable for this reason, that in his nature anger, fury, repentance, forgetting, remembering, and other things like these in no way occur. For his nature is simple, and unchangeable and undisturbed; nor is he himself one thing and what he has another, but what he has and what he is are the same. He is immortal, because he can in no way die, as the Apostle attests and says, Who alone has immortality, dwelling in light inaccessible, whom no man has seen, nor can see (I Tim. vi, 16). But wherever sacred Scripture, here and there through the divine Books, describes in God movements of the soul or human members, that is, head, hair, eyes, eyelids, ears, nostrils, mouth, lips, tongue, heart, image, womb, hands, right hand, left hand, fingers or finger, arm, wings, shoulders, back parts, feet; and likewise movements of the soul, anger, fury, forgetting, remembering, repentance, and other things like these: these are not to be understood carnally according to the literal sense by those who understand rightly, as they are by the Jews and by very many heretics of carnal mind, who suppose God to be bodily and in place; rather all things about him are to be understood and confessed spiritually. But if anyone believes that human members, or movements of the soul in human fashion, are in God, beyond doubt he fashions idols in his heart. Therefore, as has been said, when we read figuratively of a head in God, we ought to understand the very essence of his divinity, which precedes all things and to which all things are subject. The hair of his head ought to be taken typologically as the holy angels or all the elect. Of this mystery it is written in the book of the prophet Daniel, I looked until thrones were set, and the Ancient of days sat; his garment was like white snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool (Dan. vii, 9). For what is signified by his white garment is also [signified] by the hair of his head, namely the holy angels and the multitude of the saints made white. Or else his hairs are compared to clean wool so that by this he may be believed to be the Ancient of days. God is said to have eyes because he sees all things and nothing escapes him, in whose sight, as the Apostle says, no creature is invisible. For all things are naked and open to his eyes (Heb. iv, 13). In another way the eyes of the Lord are understood as the regard of his grace, as in that [verse] in the Psalm, The eyes of the Lord are upon the just (Ps. xxxiii, 16). Again, in another way the eyes of the Lord are taken mystically as his commandments, through which the light of knowledge is supplied to us, as in that [verse] in the Psalm, The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes (Ps. xviii, 9). By the eyelids of the Lord are indicated his hidden and incomprehensible judgements, or his spiritual speech in the divine Books; of these hidden and incomprehensible mysteries and judgements it is written in the Psalm, His eyelids question the sons of men (Ps. x, 5), that is, test [them]. God is said to have ears because he hears all things, and nothing escapes him under silence; of which it is written in the book of Wisdom, The ear of jealousy hears all things, and the tumult of murmurings will not be hidden (Wis. i, 10). The nostrils of God [are] his inspiration in the hearts of the faithful, as in that [verse] in the book of Kings, Smoke went up from his nostrils (II Kings xxii, 9), that is, the tearful compunction of repentance through his inspiration. The face of God [is] the knowledge of his divinity [granted] to men; of this knowledge it is written in the Psalm, Show us your face, Lord, and we shall be saved (Ps. lxxix, 4); that is, give us knowledge of you: and this knowledge became known to men through the Son, as he himself says in the Gospel, No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal [him] (Matt. xi, 27). In another way the face of God signifies the invisible essence of the divinity of the Son of God; of which the Lord himself, answering Moses through an angel, says, You will see my back parts, but my face you will not be able to see (Exod. xxxiii, 23); as if he said, You will see my incarnation in the last days, but my divinity you will not be able to see. The mouth of God [is] the Son of God the Father, that is, Christ the Lord; of whom the prophet Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Jews, says, For we provoked his mouth to anger (Lam. i, 18). In another way the mouth of the Lord is taken as his word or command; of this word of the Lord the aforesaid prophet says, The mouth of the Lord has spoken (Isa. lviii, 14); that is, the Word of God, the Son of the Father, through whom all things were made; of whom [it is said] in the Psalm, By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established (Ps. xxxii, 6). And elsewhere, He sent his Word, and healed them (Ps. cvi, 20). And in the Gospel, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John i, 1). The tongue of God mystically signifies the Holy Spirit, through whom God the Father has made his secret manifest to men; hence in the Psalm, My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly (Ps. xliv, 2). The lips of the Lord are understood as the harmony of both Testaments; of these two Testaments it is written in Proverbs, Divination is on his lips, his mouth has not erred in judgement (Prov. xvi, 10). The arms of God the Father are understood as his Son and the Holy Spirit, as in that [verse] in the prophet Isaiah, And my arms will judge the peoples (Isa. li, 5). The arm of God the Father, in the singular, is taken as his Son; of whom the prophet Jeremiah says to him, And now, Lord God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm (Jer. xxxii, 21). And the Son of God the Father is called his arm for this reason, that every elect creature is held together by him. The right hand of God the Father is taken as the same only-begotten Son; of whom it says in the Psalm, in the person of the man assumed, The right hand of the Lord has done mightily, the right hand of the Lord has exalted me (Ps. cxvii, 16). In another way the right hand of the Lord signifies the glory of the Father, that is, eternal blessedness; of which [it is said] in the Psalm, in the person of the Father to the Son, Sit at my right hand (Ps. cix, 1). Every elect creature in heaven and on earth is also called the right hand of God, just as by his left hand is understood the reprobate creature, that is, the demons and all the wicked, who, placed on the left, will undergo eternal punishments. The hand of God the Father is taken as the Son of God, because through him all things were made, as in that [verse] in the prophet Isaiah, My hand made all these things (Isa. lxvi, 2), and all things were made. In another way the hand of God is understood as his power; of this power it is written in the book of Jeremiah, As clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel (Jer. xviii, 6). Again, the hand of God is taken as the scourge; of his striking it is written in the prophet Zephaniah, I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and I will destroy from this place the remnants of Baal, etc. (Zeph. i, 4). Concerning this striking of the Lord blessed Job says of himself, The hand of the Lord has touched me (Job xix, 21). The finger of God, in the singular, is taken as the Holy Spirit, by which Holy Spirit the Law is related to have been written on two tablets of stone on Mount Sinai. For he who dictated what was to be written also wrote it, that is, the Holy Spirit; of which Holy Spirit the Lord says in the Gospel, If I cast out demons by the finger of God (Luke xi, 20). Which another evangelist, declaring it openly, says, If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God (Matt. xii, 28). For just as a finger with the hand or arm, and the hand or arm with the body, are one in nature, so the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are indeed three persons, but one substance of divinity. The fingers of God, in the plural, are understood as the holy Prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit by his inspiration wrote down the books of the Law and the Prophets; of whom it is written in the Psalm, I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers (Ps. viii, 4). For by the heavens he mystically suggested the books of the Law and the Prophets, and by the fingers, as has been said, the holy Prophets. The image of the invisible God the Father is his only-begotten Son, of whom the Apostle says, Who is the image of the invisible God (Col. i, 15). For the image of God the Father is in one way in his Son, whom he begot not from elsewhere but from himself, that is, from his own substance, like himself in all things and equal; but in another way in the soul of man, which he did not beget from himself, that is, from his substance, as very many heretics have supposed, but created from nothing. Just as the image of any king is in one way in his son, whom he begot from himself like himself, that is, a man [begetting] a man; but in another way in his ring, or his image impressed in wax, which is not what he himself is, as the son, who by nature is what the father also is. The heart of God the Father mystically indicates the secret of his wisdom, out of which he begot the Word, that is, his Son, impassibly and without beginning, as he himself says through the prophet, My heart has uttered a good word (Ps. xliv, 2). God is read to have wings because, in the manner of a bird, he gathers his elect under himself like chicks, warms [them], and protects [them] from the snares of the devil and of evil men; of his protection the Prophet says to him in the Psalm, Protect me under the shadow of your wings (Ps. xvi, 8). God is said to have shoulders because he patiently carries the weak members of the Church as if on his shoulders, and by carrying protects [them]; of which it is said in the Psalm to the just man, He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you will hope (Ps. xc, 4). The belly of God the Father is taken as the secret origin of his substance, from which origin he ineffably begot his Son before every creature, as he himself bears witness through the prophet and says, that is, the Father to the Son, From the womb before the morning star I begot you (Ps. cix, 3). In another way the womb of God mystically suggests his incomprehensible and hidden judgements, which cannot be searched out; of these hidden judgements of his it is written in Job, From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven (Job xxxviii, 29)? The back parts of the Son of God are taken as his incarnation, which took place in the last time for the redemption of the human race; of this hinder part the Son of God, speaking to Moses through an angel on Mount Sinai, says, You will see my back parts, but my face you will not be able to see (Exod. xxxiii, 23); as if he said to him, You will see my incarnation, you will not be able to see my deity. The feet of God are the firm foundation of his strength and power, because he is present everywhere and all things are subject to him, as he himself says through the prophet Isaiah, Heaven is my seat, and the earth the footstool of my feet (Isa. lxvi, 1). In another way the feet of the Son of God are understood as his incarnation, which is subject to the divinity as the feet to the head, or else because this incarnation took place towards the end of the world. For just as by the head, as has been said, his divinity is expressed, so by the feet figuratively his humanity; of this humanity it is written in Exodus, They saw the God of Israel, that is, Moses and Aaron and Nadab and Abihu and seventy of the elders of the people, and under his feet as it were a work of sapphire stone, and as it were the sky when it is clear (Exod. xxiv, 10). And just as by the sapphire stone he wished figuratively to show the heavenly creatures, that is, the holy angels, so by the clear sky [he wished to show] the holy Church of the elect taken from among men. Over these two creations the man assumed by the Son of God reigns for ever. Of whom it says in the Psalm, All things under his feet (Ps. viii, 8). In another way, by the feet of the Lord, that is, of Jesus Christ, the holy preachers are signified, of whom it is written in Deuteronomy, Those who draw near to his feet will receive of his teaching (Deut. xxxiii, 3). The garment of the Son of God is sometimes taken figuratively in the divine Books as his flesh, which was assumed by the divinity; of this clothing of his flesh the prophet Isaiah, prophesying, says, Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah (Isa. lxiii, 1)? Again, by the garments of the same Lord the holy Church is understood, which is joined to him through faith and love; of which it is written in the Psalm, The Lord has reigned, he has put on beauty (Ps. xcii, 1); and in another psalm, to the Lord himself, You have put on praise and beauty, wrapped in light as in a garment (Ps. ciii, 2). The cloak of Christ is rightly understood as his Church already mentioned; of which it is written in the book of Genesis, He will wash his robe in wine, that is, his flesh in the blood of the passion; and his cloak in the blood of the grape (Gen. xlix, 11), that is, his Church. The shoes of our Lord Jesus Christ mystically signify his incarnation, which he deigned to assume from the mortality of the human race; of this incarnation of his he himself says through the Prophet in the Psalm, Into Idumea I will stretch out my shoe (Ps. lix, 10): that is, to the people of the Gentiles I will make my incarnation manifest. The steps of God [are] the coming of the Son of God into the world, and his return to the Father; of these steps the Psalmist sang, Your steps have been seen, O God, the steps of my God, the king who is in the holy place (Ps. lxvii, 25). For he came from heaven into the womb of the virgin, and from the womb, by being born, he was laid in a manger. And after he had fulfilled all the things for which he had come, sent by the Father, he was hung on the wood of the cross; and taken down from the cross, he was buried according to the flesh, but according to the soul he descended to the lower world; and on the third day, through the power of his divinity, he raised his flesh from the tomb; and after the days of his resurrection, namely on the fortieth day, he ascended into heaven as the Apostles watched (Acts i, 9), and sits at the right hand of the Father, that is, in his glory. For these are the steps of the Son of God, this descent and ascent of his which is often read in the sacred Scriptures. God is said to ascend when the Son of God led the flesh taken from us into heaven as a captive; as is that [verse] in the Psalm, He ascended on high, he led captivity captive (Ps. lxvii, 19); because, taking up the nature of the human race, which was held captive in the world by the devil, he carried it away with him as a captive into heaven, where it had never been before. God is read to hide his face when, because their faults demand it, he hides knowledge of himself from certain reprobates; as we now see fulfilled in the people of the Jews, who, denying the Son of God, lost the knowledge of the true God, so that they became like the Gentiles, who did not know God. God is said to show his face when, with the regard of his grace, he makes himself known to those he wills, namely his elect, in their hearts by a hidden inspiration, and pours in his love so that they love him. God is said to sit, not bodily in human fashion, but [meaning that he] presides in power over every rational creature; as is that [verse] in the Psalm, The Lord has reigned over the nations, God sits upon his holy seat (Ps. xlvi, 9). God is also said to sit upon the Cherubim, which is interpreted 'fullness' or 'multitude of knowledge', by which are signified the holy angels, or the minds of spiritual men, in whom God invisibly presides and reigns. For he sits in those who are full of knowledge and love of him. For in the Proverbs of Solomon it is written, The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom. And the Wisdom of God the Father is Christ, who is said to sit in the souls of the just. God is read to descend into the world when he works something new in the human creature that was not there before; as the Son of God the Father is related to have descended when he took true flesh from the virgin Mary for our redemption, and deigned to become true man, not losing what he was, but assuming what he was not; of his descent, that is, his incarnation, it is written in the Psalm, He bowed the heavens and came down, and darkness was under his feet (Ps. xvii, 10). He bowed the heavens because before his coming he sent angels or prophets as heralds, to announce his coming to men. Darkness was under his feet because impious men, blinded by their own wickedness, could not recognise his incarnation; nor can they now. God is said to stand when he patiently bears with us, the weak, that is, his creation, [waiting] for repentance and conversion of life; as is that [verse] in the prophet Habakkuk, He stood, and measured the earth, and loosed the nations (Hab. iii, 6); that is, he stood to come to [their] aid, and loosed those who believe in him from the chains of sins. God is said to pass over when, from the hearts of certain men in whom he was formerly believed to dwell through faith, he afterwards withdraws, as unbelief or some other offence creeps in, and passes over to others. Just as God is said to withdraw from the Jews to the Gentiles, and from heretics to catholics, or from any irreligious and negligent people because of their vice, and to pass over to others, which he is accustomed to do not locally or visibly but invisibly, by a hidden and just judgement. God is said to walk, not by passing from place to place, which it is impious to believe; but his walking about is to take delight in the hearts of the saints; as it is written, And I will dwell in them, and walk among them, and I will be their God (Lev. xxvi, 12). Or indeed God's walking is to pass from place to place in his holy preachers. God's speaking is to inspire, invisibly, without sound of voice or any noise, secretly in the minds of the saints, his will and right understanding, or to reveal future things, as to the holy prophets. This speaking of God, as some hold, is taken in three ways. In the first way, through a subject creature, as he appeared to Moses in the bush and the fire; or as he deigned to appear in angels to Abraham and Jacob, or to the said Moses and the other saints to whom he willed. In the second way, in dreams, as to Jacob and to the prophet Zechariah, and to Joseph the spouse of Mary, and to other saints to whom he willed to reveal secrets. In the third way, neither through a visible creature nor through a dream, but only by hidden inspiration, invisibly touching the hearts of the saints, he makes them speak, as is read in the books of the Prophets, when the Prophets themselves, suddenly breathed upon by the divine Spirit, cried out, saying, Thus says the Lord. God's seeing is to approve good deeds; as is that [verse] in Genesis, God saw all that he had made, and they were very good (Gen. i, 31); that is, he showed to those who understand that they were good. In another way God's seeing is, by knowing, to condemn the evils of men, as is that [verse] in the prophet Isaiah, And the Lord saw, and it appeared evil in his eyes (Isa. lix, 15). Likewise, in another way God's seeing is to make us see, that is, know; as is that [verse] in the Psalm, Test me, Lord, and know my heart; question me, and know my paths, and see if the way of iniquity is in me, etc. (Ps. cxxxviii, 23). This manner of speaking is likewise found in the book of blessed Job, where concerning the Wisdom of God the Father, after he had said many remarkable things about God the Father, he added: Then he saw it, and declared it, and searched it out, and prepared it (Job xxviii, 27); that is, he made [men] see and proclaim and search out and announce [it] to others. God's knowing is to make [men] know, as he himself says to Abraham, Now I know that you fear God (Gen. xxii, 12). For he did not come to know in time who knows all things before they happen; but God is said to know [meaning] to make [men] know, so that those who were before unknown to themselves as to what they were might become manifest to themselves through his questioning, that is, his testing. Such too is that [verse] in the law of Moses concerning the people of Israel, That I may test them, he says, whether they keep my commandments or not (Deut. xiii, 3). God's not knowing is to reject certain reprobates; as is that [verse] in the Gospel, I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you who work iniquity (Luke xiii, 27; Ps. vi, 9). God is said to be jealous when he often chastises, rebukes and scourges his creature, which he does not want to perish, and by scourging brings it back to himself. Or indeed God is said to be jealous in that he wills to leave no sin unpunished. For he is just, and therefore all injustice is abhorrent to him, which, as has been said, he in no way allows to go unpunished. God is said to be angry, not by a motion of the mind or any disturbance, which cannot happen to him at all; but he is said to inflict just vengeance on the creature that offends, that is, on impious men and sinners, that is, to render to them what they deserve: and this divine vengeance is called his anger or fury. God is said to repent, not that he repents of his past works in the manner of men; for he who knows all things before they happen cannot repent of his past deeds; but God's repentance is to change what was decreed, and to change into something else what had first been begun otherwise; that is, either from good into evil, as their faults demand, as it is read of Saul that God repented that he had made him king (1 Kgs xv, 11); or as we now see done in the people of the Jews, who, though they were the people of God, because of their impiety became the synagogue of Satan; or from evil into good, as happened in the people of the Gentiles, who before were not the people of God, but now through the grace of Christ have been made the people of God. In this way indeed, by the hidden judgement of God, Judas the traitor fell from the rank of apostleship and was plunged into the abyss of hell, while the thief, after the crime of robbery, was transferred from the cross to paradise. This change too, from good to evil, as has been said, or from evil to good, which comes about by the hidden and just judgement of God, whether through the severity of his justice or through his mercy, we call the repentance of God. This is written more explicitly in the book of the prophet Jeremiah. God's not repenting is in no way to change what was decreed; as is that [verse] in the Psalm, The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent; that is, the Father to the Son, You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. cix, 4). The Son of God is called priest of the Father, not according to his divinity but according to his humanity, in which he offered himself for us through his passion and death as an acceptable sacrifice to God the Father, so that he himself should be the priest who is also the sacrifice. God is said to forget when he does not have mercy on certain impious men and sinners, which he certainly does not do through cruelty, which is not in God, but through his hidden and just judgement. God is said to harden the hearts of certain wicked men, as is written of Pharaoh king of Egypt: not that almighty God by his power hardens their hearts, which it is impious to believe; but when, as their faults demand, he does not take away the hardness of heart which they themselves nourish by doing evil, he is said himself to harden them, because by just judgement he allows them to be hardened. God's sleeping is when the only-begotten Son of the Father deigned to die for us in the flesh he had assumed; whose death is rightly proclaimed a sweet sleep, as he himself says through the prophet Jeremiah, Therefore I was as one roused from sleep; and I saw, and my sleep was sweet to me (Jer. xxxi, 26). In another way God is said to sleep when faith in him, amid the prosperity of this world, does not keep watch in the heart of certain believers, but sleeps. Our Saviour signified this sleeping in himself when he slept in the boat amid the waves of the sea (Matt. viii, 24). Or indeed God's sleeping is to come late to the aid of his elect placed in the tribulations of this world, as is that [verse] in the Psalm, Arise, why do you sleep, Lord (Ps. xliii, 23)? God's keeping watch is to show himself openly in the defence of his elect and in vengeance on his enemies.

II. All these things that have been mentioned above, and others like them, which holy Scripture narrates about God according to the historical sense, are to be taken not according to the letter, as has been said, but as figurative speech: because almighty God in the essence of his divinity is spirit, not flesh; invisible and incorporeal, and composed of no human members: and therefore he is to be contemplated not with the eyes of the flesh, but with the eyes of the heart. God is wisdom, he is truth, he is charity, he is justice; and therefore he is to be seen with the same eyes with which all these things are contemplated: and therefore he is to be beheld by the faithful not with bodily sight, as has been said, but from a pure heart. For it is written in the Gospel, Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt. v, 8). For this is the reward of the saints, promised not in this life only, but rather in the life to come; as the blessed apostle John says, Beloved, we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. For we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John iii, 2). This promise, as has been said, is laid up for the saints in the world to come, after the resurrection of the flesh and the judgement of God. But in the present life no one of the elect of God is so holy, no one so perfect, that he has ever seen, or will be able to see, the Lord himself in the essence of his divinity as he is: as he himself testifies to Moses, For man shall not see me and live (Exod. xxxiii, 20); as if he were saying, No one, as long as he lives mortally, will be able to see God as he is. For the saints in the present life see God, not as he is in his substance, but through a mirror and in a riddle, but afterwards face to face (1 Cor. xiii, 12). They see in this life by believing, not by discerning with bodily eyes. For to see God is to believe in him rightly and to love him from the heart. This indeed is what the name Israel signifies, which is interpreted, A man seeing God. But since the Son of God, who in the substance of divinity is one with the Father, for the restoration of the human race which had fallen in Adam, near the end of the world entered into the womb of the virgin Mary, created true flesh from her substance, and so united [it] in the singleness of his person that he was God and man alike; and was born, in a single person, as has been said, but a twofold substance, from the same virgin with her chastity uncorrupted; so that he who was and is in his divinity true God, begotten of the true Father, invisible, incorporeal and incomprehensible as is the Father also, should himself be also true man, visible, bodily, and circumscribed; and the very same, not one God and another man, but God and man, one Christ the Son of God, suffered for our salvation, died and was buried in the flesh alone, in the same flesh in which also on the third day, rising from the tomb by the power of his divinity, he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father: whom the universal Church awaits to come from there to judge the living and the dead, in the same flesh in which he ascended, but glorified, as all the faithful sing in the Creed; therefore it is right to believe and confess the same Son of God, according to the substance of his divinity, to be invisible and incorporeal and immortal and uncircumscribed, as are also the Father and the Holy Spirit: but according to his humanity it is fitting to believe and confess [him] to be visible, bodily, in a place, and truly having all human members. For just as it is impious not to believe the same Son of God and our redeemer to be, according to his divinity, invisible and incorporeal, as are also the Father and the Holy Spirit: so it is profane not to believe and profess the same Son of God, in the man assumed, to be visible and bodily and in a place after the resurrection. But that which is written in Genesis, when God the Father says to the Son, Let us make man to our image and likeness (Gen. i, 26), is not to be taken as if God were bodily and composed of the outlines of members, and had made our outer man, that is the human body, after that bodily composition, as if after his own likeness; as the Jews and many other unbelievers have supposed, which it is impious to believe. But God, as has often been said, is spirit, not flesh: he is wisdom, not body. For God made man to his image not in the body, but in the soul; not in the body, but in the understanding; not in the outer man, but in reason. And the soul of man, as has been said, is held to have been made to the image of God for this reason, that it is a spiritual creature, invisible and incorporeal and immortal: not drawing its origin from the substance of God, as the heretics the Manichaeans and Priscillianists falsely supposed; but created by God from nothing. It has a beginning, but knows no end. This human soul, because it was made rational and intellectual by God, is said to be the image of God. For there is in it by nature a rational sense, through which it understands, is wise, and discerns between good and evil. There is in it memory, through which it recalls things past: there is will, through which it chooses what it wishes: there is sense, through which it also perceives: there is reason, through which it contemplates things both hidden and invisible, through which it understands God its creator, through which it discerns true things from false, through which it contemplates or beholds invisible things and God with the eyes of the heart. In all these the soul of man is related to have been made to the image of God: all these it has in common with the angels, but the body with the brute animals which lack understanding. The origin of this soul is hidden, and known to God alone. The soul of man too, because it is a spiritual creature, is in holy Scripture sometimes called spirit, sometimes nature, sometimes also life, and sometimes it is said to be the heart: and though it is one in its nature, it has received different names because of its various effects. But the likeness of God in man refers to the work of justice, as the Lord says in the Law, Be holy, because I the Lord your God am holy (Lev. xix, 2). Instructing us about this holiness, the blessed apostle Paul says, Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth (Eph. iv, 23). And again he himself [says], Be imitators of me, as I also [am] of Christ (1 Cor. xi, 1). And blessed John, exhorting, says, He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked (1 John ii, 6). And the Truth [says] in the Gospel, Be merciful, as your heavenly Father also is merciful (Luke vi, 36). For just as the image of God pertains to the nature of the soul, so too the likeness refers to the work of justice.
